label: Digitally Immersed & Emotionally Strained
summary: This profile represents highly educated women who spend substantial time on social media (averaging nearly 4 hours daily, with many exceeding 5 hours) and report elevated levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety. Across all three psychological well-being measures—loneliness (UCLA-8 mean 1.78), depression (PHQ-9 mean 1.81), and anxiety (GAD-7 mean 2.27)—scores are notably higher than typical, suggesting a cluster of co-occurring emotional difficulties alongside heavy digital engagement.
demographic_anchor: Female, graduate-level education or above, daily social-media use exceeding 5 hours
behavior_markers: Heavy daily social-media consumption averaging approximately 3.9 hours with a substantial proportion exceeding 5 hours
Elevated self-reported loneliness consistent with moderate UCLA-8 scores
Moderate-to-high depressive symptomatology as indicated by PHQ-9 responses
Notably high anxiety symptoms with GAD-7 scores averaging above 2.2
Pattern of co-occurring psychological distress across multiple domains alongside intensive digital media use
tone: Concerned and empathetic; the data point to meaningful emotional burden in a highly educated, digitally engaged group that may benefit from targeted well-being support

label: Well-Adjusted Light-Use Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents male respondents with graduate-level education who report notably low levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms. Their daily social media use is relatively light, averaging roughly 2.8 hours per day (within the 1–3 hour bracket). Across all psychological well-being indicators, this group scores well below scale midpoints, suggesting generally positive mental health and moderate digital engagement.
demographic_anchor: Male, graduate degree or above, 1–3 hours of daily social media use
behavior_markers: Low loneliness scores (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 0.78, well below scale midpoint)
Minimal depressive symptomatology (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 0.27, near floor)
Very low anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 mean ≈ 0.03, near floor)
Light daily social media consumption averaging approximately 2.8 hours
Consistent pattern of psychological well-being across all measured dimensions

label: Lonely but Low-Distress Heavy Social-Media User
summary: This profile captures highly educated women who report elevated loneliness yet comparatively low levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms, despite spending nearly five hours per day on social media. Their loneliness scores sit above the sample norm while their PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores remain modest, suggesting that heavy social-media engagement may coexist with emotional isolation without necessarily escalating into clinical-level mood or anxiety disorders.
demographic_anchor: Female, graduate-level education or above, approximately 3–5 hours of daily social-media use
behavior_markers: Elevated loneliness (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 1.30) relative to other profiles
Below-average depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 0.90)
Below-average anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 mean ≈ 0.85)
Heavy daily social-media use averaging close to 5 hours (midpoint ≈ 4.89 hours)
Possible pattern of using social media as a substitute for in-person social connection without marked psychological distress
tone: Quietly disconnected; socially active online yet personally isolated, maintaining emotional composure despite unmet belonging needs

label: Well-Adjusted Light-Use Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents a relatively large group (n=217) of male respondents with graduate-level education who report low levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms. Their daily social-media use is light, averaging roughly 1.6 hours per day (within the 1–3 hour range). Across all psychological well-being indicators, this group scores well below scale midpoints, suggesting generally positive mental health and moderate digital engagement.

behavior_markers: Light daily social-media usage averaging approximately 1.6 hours
